claim: Chronic inhalation of cigarette smoke is the major cause of sterile inflammation and pulmonary emphysema.
source: Chronic inhalation of cigarette smoke is the major cause of sterile inflammation and pulmonary emphysema.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge in the abstract.

claim: Insoluble nanoparticulate carbon black (nCB) accumulates in human myeloid dendritic cells (mDCs) from emphysematous lung.
source: In this study, we show that insoluble nanoparticulate carbon black (nCB) accumulates in human myeloid dendritic cells (mDCs) from emphysematous lung and in CD11c+ lung antigen presenting cells (APC) of mice exposed to smoke.
evidence: Supported by experimental observations using Raman spectroscopy, hyperspectral imaging, and HR-TEM as described in the Results section.

claim: nCB accumulates in CD11c+ lung antigen presenting cells (APC) of mice exposed to smoke.
source: In this study, we show that insoluble nanoparticulate carbon black (nCB) accumulates in human myeloid dendritic cells (mDCs) from emphysematous lung and in CD11c+ lung antigen presenting cells (APC) of mice exposed to smoke.
evidence: Supported by experimental data from mouse smoke exposure models.

claim: nCB intranasal administration induced emphysema in mouse lungs.
source: Likewise, nCB intranasal administration induced emphysema in mouse lungs.
evidence: Supported by experimental data showing lung volume increases, MLI measurements, and histological changes.

claim: nCB persisted indefinitely in mouse lung when delivered by smoking or intranasally.
source: Delivered by smoking or intranasally, nCB persisted indefinitely in mouse lung, activated lung APCs, and promoted T helper 17 cell differentiation through double-stranded DNA break (DSB) and ASC-mediated inflammasome assembly in phagocytes.
evidence: Supported by long-term follow-up data showing nCB presence at 7 and 18 months after exposure.

claim: nCB activated lung APCs.
source: Delivered by smoking or intranasally, nCB persisted indefinitely in mouse lung, activated lung APCs, and promoted T helper 17 cell differentiation through double-stranded DNA break (DSB) and ASC-mediated inflammasome assembly in phagocytes.
evidence: Supported by data showing increased cytokine production and activation markers in APCs exposed to nCB.

claim: nCB promoted T helper 17 cell differentiation through double-stranded DNA break (DSB) and ASC-mediated inflammasome assembly in phagocytes.
source: Delivered by smoking or intranasally, nCB persisted indefinitely in mouse lung, activated lung APCs, and promoted T helper 17 cell differentiation through double-stranded DNA break (DSB) and ASC-mediated inflammasome assembly in phagocytes.
evidence: Supported by experimental data showing γH2AX expression, inflammasome activation, and Th17 cell increases.

claim: Increasing the polarity or size of CB mitigated many adverse effects.
source: Increasing the polarity or size of CB mitigated many adverse effects.
evidence: Supported by experimental data comparing nCB with PEG-nCB and different particle sizes.

claim: nCB causes sterile inflammation, DSB, and emphysema.
source: Thus, nCB causes sterile inflammation, DSB, and emphysema and explains adverse health outcomes seen in smokers while implicating the dangers of nCB exposure in non-smokers.
evidence: Supported by comprehensive experimental data throughout the study.

claim: Tobacco smoking is linked to a long and growing list of fatal illnesses (e.g., emphysema, cancer, and stroke).
source: Tobacco smoking is linked to a long and growing (Barnes, 2014; Carter et al., 2015) list of fatal illnesses (e.g., emphysema, cancer, and stroke) and is the major preventable cause of human death.
evidence: Supported by citations to published literature.

claim: Tobacco smoking is the major preventable cause of human death.
source: Tobacco smoking is linked to a long and growing (Barnes, 2014; Carter et al., 2015) list of fatal illnesses (e.g., emphysema, cancer, and stroke) and is the major preventable cause of human death.
evidence: Supported by citations and established public health knowledge.

claim: In many large developing countries the prevalence of smoking is growing.
source: Despite public awareness of the harmful effects of smoking, in many large developing countries the prevalence of smoking is growing (Eriksen et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by citation to published literature.

claim: The molecular mechanism underlying emphysema and its persistence despite smoking cessation remains unclear.
source: While our understanding of the immune basis of smoke-induced sterile inflammation has increased, the molecular mechanism underlying emphysema and its persistence despite smoking cessation remains unclear (Cosio et al., 2009; Kheradmand et al., 2012).
evidence: Stated as a knowledge gap in the field, supported by citations.

claim: Less is known regarding the health-related inhalation effects of atmospheric and workplace airborne carbon particulates.
source: Even less is known regarding the health-related inhalation effects of atmospheric and workplace airborne carbon particulates.
evidence: Stated as a knowledge gap in the field.

claim: Innate immune cells such as alveolar macrophages and neutrophils are recruited to the lungs in response to cigarette smoke.
source: Innate immune cells such as alveolar macrophages and neutrophils are recruited to the lungs in response to cigarette smoke (Salvi, 2014).
evidence: Supported by citation to published literature.

claim: Several human studies and pre-clinical models of smoke-induced emphysema have confirmed that lymphocytes (T and B cells) and lung antigen presenting cells (APCs) play pathogenic roles in chronic lung inflammation in smokers.
source: Several human studies and pre-clinical models of smoke-induced emphysema have also confirmed that lymphocytes (T and B cells) and lung antigen presenting cells (APCs) play pathogenic roles in chronic lung inflammation in smokers (Shan et al., 2009, 2014; Churg et al., 2012b).
evidence: Supported by citations to published literature.

claim: Increased concentrations of pro-inflammatory cytokines such as IL-6, IL-1β, and IL-17A are among the most important hallmarks of smoke-mediated lung inflammation.
source: Prior work has shown that increased concentrations of pro-inflammatory cytokines such as IL-6, IL-1β, and IL-17A are among the most important hallmarks of smoke-mediated lung inflammation (Shan et al., 2009, 2014; Chang et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by citations to published literature.

claim: IL-17A plays a critical role in smoke-induced emphysema in humans and in mouse models of disease.
source: We and others have previously shown that IL-17A plays a critical role in smoke-induced emphysema in humans and in mouse models of disease (Shan et al., 2012; Kurimoto et al., 2013; Zhang et al., 2013; Chang et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by citations to published literature including authors' own work.

claim: Adoptive transfer of lineage-negative CD11c+ myeloid dendritic cells (mDCs) isolated from the lungs of smoke-exposed mice to naive mice recapitulates smoke-induced lung disease.
source: Further, adoptive transfer of lineage-negative CD11c+ myeloid dendritic cells (mDCs) isolated from the lungs of smoke-exposed mice to naive mice recapitulates smoke-induced lung disease, indicating a direct causal relationship between mDC and emphysema (Shan et al., 2012).
evidence: Supported by citation to published literature.

claim: There is a direct causal relationship between mDC and emphysema.
source: Further, adoptive transfer of lineage-negative CD11c+ myeloid dendritic cells (mDCs) isolated from the lungs of smoke-exposed mice to naive mice recapitulates smoke-induced lung disease, indicating a direct causal relationship between mDC and emphysema (Shan et al., 2012).
evidence: Inferred from adoptive transfer experiments cited.

claim: The mechanism by which smoke induces the inflammatory mDC phenotype remains completely unknown.
source: Despite these advances, the mechanism by which smoke induces the inflammatory mDC phenotype remains completely unknown.
evidence: Stated as a knowledge gap in the field.

claim: Tobacco smoke contains many noxious chemicals (e.g., carbon monoxide, sulfur, nitrogen dioxide, nitric oxide, and methane), aromatics (e.g., benzene, toluene, and xylene) and chlorinated (e.g., methyl chloride, chloroethene, and chloroform) volatile organic compounds, as well as particulate matter.
source: Tobacco smoke contains many noxious chemicals (e.g., carbon monoxide, sulfur, nitrogen dioxide, nitric oxide, and methane), aromatics (e.g., benzene, toluene, and xylene) and chlorinated (e.g., methyl chloride, chloroethene, and chloroform) volatile organic compounds, as well as particulate matter (Wang et al., 2012; Perfetti and Rodgman, 2013; Salvi, 2014).
evidence: Supported by citations to published literature.

claim: One or more agents in tobacco smoke is thought to underlie the carcinogenic potential of smoke, involving at least eight different cancers.
source: One or more of these agents is thought to underlie the carcinogenic potential of smoke, involving at least eight different cancers; accordingly, the role of volatile carcinogens found in smoke has been studied extensively (Pope et al., 2011; Carter et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by citations to published literature.

claim: The role of volatile carcinogens found in smoke has been studied extensively.
source: One or more of these agents is thought to underlie the carcinogenic potential of smoke, involving at least eight different cancers; accordingly, the role of volatile carcinogens found in smoke has been studied extensively (Pope et al., 2011; Carter et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by citations to published literature.

claim: Far less is known about the pathogenic effects of particulate matter that is suspended in smoke and which includes nanoparticulate carbon, metal oxides, and inorganic salts.
source: Far less is known about the pathogenic effects of particulate matter that is suspended in smoke and which includes nanoparticulate carbon, metal oxides, and inorganic salts.
evidence: Stated as a knowledge gap in the field.

claim: Histopathological analysis of the lungs of heavy smokers invariably reveals dark-staining anthracotic pigment often attributed to poorly soluble material found in tobacco smoke.
source: Histopathological analysis of the lungs of heavy smokers invariably reveals dark-staining anthracotic pigment often attributed to poorly soluble material found in tobacco smoke (Mitchev et al., 2002).
evidence: Supported by citation to published literature.

claim: Anthracotic pigment is found in the lymph nodes of smokers.
source: Anthracotic pigment is also found in the lymph nodes of smokers (Churg et al., 2005), but its chemical composition and potential contribution to smoking-related diseases have not been explored.
evidence: Supported by citation to published literature.

claim: The chemical composition and potential contribution of anthracotic pigment to smoking-related diseases have not been explored.
source: Anthracotic pigment is also found in the lymph nodes of smokers (Churg et al., 2005), but its chemical composition and potential contribution to smoking-related diseases have not been explored.
evidence: Stated as a knowledge gap in the field.

claim: The anthracotic material found in the lung of human smokers is nanoparticulate carbon black (nCB).
source: In this study, we show that the anthracotic material found in the lung of human smokers is nanoparticulate carbon black (nCB), a hydrophobic material that accumulates specifically in highly activated CD1a+ lung APCs.
evidence: Supported by Raman spectroscopy, hyperspectral imaging, and HR-TEM data presented in the study.

claim: nCB is a hydrophobic material that accumulates specifically in highly activated CD1a+ lung APCs.
source: In this study, we show that the anthracotic material found in the lung of human smokers is nanoparticulate carbon black (nCB), a hydrophobic material that accumulates specifically in highly activated CD1a+ lung APCs.
evidence: Supported by experimental data showing nCB in CD1a+ cells from emphysematous lungs.

claim: nCB accumulates in the lung and APC of mice exposed to smoke.
source: Raman spectroscopy, hyperspectral imaging, and high-resolution transmission electron microscopy (HR-TEM) were used to confirm this observation and show that nCB further accumulates in the lung and APC of mice exposed to smoke.
evidence: Supported by experimental data using multiple analytical techniques.

claim: nCB given by inhalation to mice in amounts that are comparable to human exposures is alone sufficient to cause sterile inflammation and induce robust T helper 17 cell (Th17) responses and emphysema.
source: Moreover, we show that nCB given by inhalation to mice in amounts that are comparable to human exposures is alone sufficient to cause sterile inflammation and induce robust T helper 17 cell (Th17) responses and emphysema, implicating the potential health risks of airborne nCB that contaminates a wide range of workplace and domestic environments (IARC Working Group on the Evaluation of Carcinogenic Risks to Humans, 2010).
evidence: Supported by experimental data from mouse intranasal nCB challenge studies.

claim: The lungs of heavy smokers are typically dark brown or black in contrast to the white or pink appearance of normal lungs.
source: In contrast to the white or pink appearance of normal lungs, the lungs of heavy smokers are typically dark brown or black (Churg et al., 2005).
evidence: Supported by citation and general medical knowledge.

claim: Anthracotic pigmentation was observed in lung cells from smokers but not from non-smokers.
source: During the routine preparation of lung phagocytic cells including CD1a+ mDCs and APCs, we observed the same anthracotic pigmentation in lung cells from smokers (Figure 1A,B), whereas the same cells isolated from non-smokers lacked the pigment.
evidence: Supported by microscopic observations shown in Figure 1A,B.

claim: Activated mDCs from smokers and smoke-exposed mice promote Th1 and Th17 responses.
source: We previously showed that activated mDCs from smokers and smoke-exposed mice promote Th1 and Th17 responses (Shan et al., 2009, 2012).
evidence: Supported by citations to authors' previous work.

claim: HR-TEM of residual black material after complete proteolytic digestion of human emphysematous lung showed aggregates composed of 20–50 nm spheroids.
source: To determine the nature of the anthracotic pigment from mDCs, we first performed HR-TEM of the residual black material after complete proteolytic digestion of human emphysematous lung and observed the aggregates that were composed of 20–50 nm spheroids (Figure 1C).
evidence: Supported by HR-TEM data shown in Figure 1C.

claim: Raman spectroscopy and hyperspectral mapping of CD1a+ mDCs from human emphysematous lung tissue showed the signature for pure nCB and not inorganic salts or metal oxides.
source: To further extend these observations, we examined CD1a+ mDCs from human emphysematous lung tissue using Raman spectroscopy and hyperspectral mapping which showed the signature for pure nCB and not inorganic salts or metal oxides (Figure 1D–H).
evidence: Supported by Raman spectroscopy and hyperspectral imaging data shown in Figure 1D-H.

claim: nCB is extensively deposited as solid material in the lungs of smokers and specifically accumulates in lung APC.
source: Thus, nCB is extensively deposited as solid material in the lungs of smokers and specifically accumulates in lung APC.
evidence: Conclusion drawn from multiple analytical techniques applied to human lung samples.

claim: Isolated CD11c+ APCs and cells present in bronchoalveolar (BAL) fluid (macrophages >90%) from mice exposed to smoke for 4 months contain particulate matter with the Raman spectral signature of nCB within each cell.
source: When compared to air-exposed mice, we confirmed that isolated CD11c+ APCs and cells present in bronchoalveolar (BAL) fluid (macrophages >90%) (Shan et al., 2012) contain particulate matter with the Raman spectral signature of nCB within each cell (Figure 1I).
evidence: Supported by Raman spectroscopy data shown in Figure 1I.

claim: Both humans and mice chronically exposed to cigarette smoke accumulate nCB within phagocytic lung APCs.
source: These findings indicate that both humans and mice chronically exposed to cigarette smoke accumulate nCB within phagocytic lung APCs.
evidence: Conclusion drawn from comparative data in humans and mice.

claim: Commercial nCB does not desorb polycyclic aromatic hydrocarbons (PAHs), as determined by Soxhlet extraction followed by gas chromatography mass spectroscopy (GCMS).
source: We first determined that the commercial nCB does not desorb polycyclic aromatic hydrocarbons (PAHs), as determined by Soxhlet extraction followed by gas chromatography mass spectroscopy (GCMS) (Harwood and Moody, 1989).
evidence: Supported by GCMS analysis performed in the study.

claim: Mice exposed to nCB showed lungs that were extensively anthracotic, similar in appearance to lungs of long-term smokers.
source: 4 weeks after the last intranasal instillation of nCB, harvested lungs were extensively anthracotic, similar in appearance to lungs of long-term smokers (Figure 2A).
evidence: Supported by visual observation shown in Figure 2A.

claim: nCB challenge induced enlargement of the alveolar spaces.
source: Physiologically, the nCB challenge-induced enlargement of the alveolar spaces (Figure 2B) concomitant with significant increases in total lung volume quantified by micro-CT imaging and unbiased lung morphometry measurement (mean linear intercept; MLI) (Figure 2C,D), both hallmarks of emphysema.
evidence: Supported by histological and imaging data shown in Figure 2B-D.

claim: nCB challenge induced significant increases in total lung volume quantified by micro-CT imaging and unbiased lung morphometry measurement (mean linear intercept; MLI), both hallmarks of emphysema.
source: Physiologically, the nCB challenge-induced enlargement of the alveolar spaces (Figure 2B) concomitant with significant increases in total lung volume quantified by micro-CT imaging and unbiased lung morphometry measurement (mean linear intercept; MLI) (Figure 2C,D), both hallmarks of emphysema.
evidence: Supported by quantitative CT and morphometry data shown in Figure 2C,D.

claim: Mice exposed to nCB showed significantly increased numbers of macrophages, neutrophils, and lymphocytes in BAL fluid as compared to vehicle (PBS)-challenged control animals.
source: Mice exposed to nCB showed significantly increased numbers of macrophages, neutrophils, and lymphocytes in BAL fluid as compared to vehicle (PBS)-challenged control animals (Figure 2E).
evidence: Supported by BAL fluid cell count data shown in Figure 2E.

claim: Increased lung inflammation in nCB-exposed mice was accompanied by higher concentrations of inflammatory cytokines and chemokines.
source: Consistently, increased lung inflammation was accompanied by higher concentrations of inflammatory cytokines and chemokines (Figure 2—figure supplement 2) as well as elastolytic matrix metalloproteinases (MMPs) 9 and 12 (Figure 2F), all of which are characteristic features of cigarette smoke-induced emphysema in human patients and animal models of this disease (Shan et al., 2009; Churg et al., 2012a).
evidence: Supported by multiplex assay data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2.

claim: Increased lung inflammation in nCB-exposed mice was accompanied by higher levels of elastolytic matrix metalloproteinases (MMPs) 9 and 12.
source: Consistently, increased lung inflammation was accompanied by higher concentrations of inflammatory cytokines and chemokines (Figure 2—figure supplement 2) as well as elastolytic matrix metalloproteinases (MMPs) 9 and 12 (Figure 2F), all of which are characteristic features of cigarette smoke-induced emphysema in human patients and animal models of this disease (Shan et al., 2009; Churg et al., 2012a).
evidence: Supported by qPCR data shown in Figure 2F.

claim: Higher concentrations of inflammatory cytokines and chemokines as well as elastolytic MMPs 9 and 12 are characteristic features of cigarette smoke-induced emphysema in human patients and animal models of this disease.
source: Consistently, increased lung inflammation was accompanied by higher concentrations of inflammatory cytokines and chemokines (Figure 2—figure supplement 2) as well as elastolytic matrix metalloproteinases (MMPs) 9 and 12 (Figure 2F), all of which are characteristic features of cigarette smoke-induced emphysema in human patients and animal models of this disease (Shan et al., 2009; Churg et al., 2012a).
evidence: Supported by citations to published literature.

claim: Both lung parenchymal CD11c+ mDCs and BAL fluid macrophages showed an accumulation of nCB as detected by hyperspectral imaging.
source: Similarly, both lung parenchymal CD11c+ mDCs and BAL fluid macrophages showed an accumulation of nCB as detected by hyperspectral imaging (Figure 2G–I).
evidence: Supported by hyperspectral imaging data shown in Figure 2G-I.

claim: Gross and microscopic examination of the lungs at 7 and 18 months following the last nCB exposure showed persistence of nCB, lung inflammation, and hyperinflation.
source: Gross and microscopic examination of the lungs at 7 and 18 months following the last nCB exposure showed persistence of nCB, lung inflammation, and hyperinflation (Figure 2—figure supplement 3–5).
evidence: Supported by long-term follow-up data shown in Figure 2—figure supplements 3-5.

claim: nCB—as an insoluble byproduct of tobacco combustion—accumulates in lung and airway APCs, is poorly cleared from the lungs, and is alone sufficient to cause lung inflammation and emphysema in mice.
source: Thus, nCB—as an insoluble byproduct of tobacco combustion as shown above and also delivered through a non-smoking model—accumulates in lung and airway APCs, is poorly cleared from the lungs, and is alone sufficient to cause lung inflammation and emphysema in mice.
evidence: Conclusion drawn from comprehensive experimental data.

claim: Cigarette smoke induces lung APC activation in human patients and mice, which then induces Th17 cell differentiation in naive T cells.
source: We previously determined that cigarette smoke induces lung APC activation in human patients and mice, which then induces Th17 cell differentiation in naive T cells (Shan et al., 2009).
evidence: Supported by citation to authors' previous work.

claim: Lung CD11c+CD11bhi mDCs were significantly increased in the lungs of nCB-challenged mice when compared with controls.
source: Lung CD11c+CD11bhi mDCs were significantly increased in the lungs of nCB-challenged mice when compared with controls (Figure 3A,B).
evidence: Supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 3A,B.

claim: nCB selectively induced lung Th17 but not Th1 responses relative to control animals.
source: nCB also selectively induced lung Th17 but not Th1 responses relative to control animals (Figure 3C,D and Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Supported by intracellular cytokine staining data shown in Figure 3C,D and Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: Lung CD11c+ APCs isolated from nCB-challenged mice secreted significantly more of the Th17 cell growth factors IL-6 and IL-1β, along with other pro-inflammatory cytokines and chemokines, but not IL-12 or IL-4.
source: Lung CD11c+ APCs isolated from nCB-challenged mice secreted significantly more of the Th17 cell growth factors IL-6 and IL-1β, along with other pro-inflammatory cytokines and chemokines, but not IL-12 or IL-4 (IL-4 was undetectable in both PBS and nCB groups), which promote Th1 and Th2 cell differentiation, respectively (Figure 3—figure supplement 2).
evidence: Supported by multiplex assay data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2.

claim: IL-12 and IL-4 promote Th1 and Th2 cell differentiation, respectively.
source: Lung CD11c+ APCs isolated from nCB-challenged mice secreted significantly more of the Th17 cell growth factors IL-6 and IL-1β, along with other pro-inflammatory cytokines and chemokines, but not IL-12 or IL-4 (IL-4 was undetectable in both PBS and nCB groups), which promote Th1 and Th2 cell differentiation, respectively (Figure 3—figure supplement 2).
evidence: Established immunological knowledge.

claim: Lung APCs from nCB-challenged mice induced significantly more IL-17A, but neither IFN-γ nor IL-4 production, when compared to controls in co-culture with naive splenic CD4+ T cells.
source: Lung APCs from nCB-challenged mice induced significantly more IL-17A, but neither IFN-γ nor IL-4 production, when compared to controls (Figure 3—figure supplement 3).
evidence: Supported by ELISA data from co-culture experiments shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 3.

claim: Lung Th17 responses persisted for at least 7 months following the last nCB challenge.
source: Lung Th17 responses persisted for at least 7 months following the last nCB challenge (Figure 3—figure supplement 4).
evidence: Supported by long-term follow-up data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 4.

claim: Il-17a−/− mice were resistant to nCB challenge as assessed by their attenuated increases in lung volume, lung immune cell infiltration, and the reduced destruction of alveoli when compared to identically treated WT mice.
source: Further, Il-17a−/− mice were resistant to nCB challenge as assessed by their attenuated increases in lung volume, lung immune cell infiltration, and the reduced destruction of alveoli (Figure 3E–H) when compared to identically treated WT mice.
evidence: Supported by data from Il-17a−/− mice shown in Figure 3E-H.

claim: In vivo nCB selectively induces chronic lung Th17 responses, which are crucial for CB-induced emphysema in mice.
source: Thus, in vivo nCB selectively induces chronic lung Th17 responses, which are crucial for CB-induced emphysema in mice.
evidence: Conclusion drawn from Il-17a−/− mouse experiments and other data.

claim: nCB treatment significantly inhibited Treg differentiation.
source: However, nCB treatment significantly inhibited Treg differentiation (Figure 3—figure supplement 5A,B).
evidence: Supported by in vitro T cell differentiation data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 5A,B.

claim: nCB did not affect Th1 or Th17 cell differentiation directly.
source: We found that nCB did not affect Th1 or Th17 cell differentiation directly (Figure 3—figure supplement 5A).
evidence: Supported by in vitro T cell differentiation data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 5A.

claim: nCB promotes sterile inflammation by inducing Th17 differentiation indirectly through APCs and directly by inhibiting Treg differentiation.
source: These findings indicate that nCB promotes sterile inflammation by inducing Th17 differentiation indirectly through APCs and directly by inhibiting Treg differentiation.
evidence: Conclusion drawn from in vitro T cell differentiation experiments.

claim: Conjugating polyethylene glycol to nCB (PEG-nCB) renders the material hydrophilic and miscible with aqueous solutions.
source: Conjugating polyethylene glycol to nCB (PEG-nCB) renders the material hydrophilic and miscible with aqueous solutions (Hwang et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by citation and chemical modification performed in the study.

claim: Mice challenged with intranasal PEG-nCB failed to develop emphysema as assessed by quantitative CT-based lung volume measurements, MLI and microscopic evaluation of the lungs.
source: Mice challenged with intranasal PEG-nCB using the same protocol (Figure 2—figure supplement 1) failed to develop emphysema as assessed by quantitative CT-based lung volume measurements, MLI and microscopic evaluation of the lungs (Figure 4A,B,C).
evidence: Supported by CT, morphometry, and histology data shown in Figure 4A-C.

claim: Less anthracotic pigment was detected in the lung parenchyma of PEG-nCB-challenged mice, suggesting that in contrast to hydrophobic nCB, PEG-nCB could be cleared from the lungs.
source: Further, we detected less anthracotic pigment in the lung parenchyma, suggesting that in contrast to hydrophobic nCB, PEG-nCB could be cleared from the lungs (Figure 4C).
evidence: Observation from histology with inference about clearance.

claim: Microscopic inspection of isolated BAL fluid cells from PEG-nCB-challenged mice showed intact phagocytic cells compared to that of hydrophobic nCB, suggesting that the latter may induce less cytotoxic effects on phagocytic cells.
source: Microscopic inspection of isolated BAL fluid cells from PEG-nCB-challenged mice showed intact phagocytic cells compared to that of hydrophobic nCB, suggesting that the latter may induce less cytotoxic effects on phagocytic cells (Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Observation from microscopy with inference about cytotoxicity.

claim: The release of lactate dehydrogenase (LDH), an indicator of cytotoxicity, was enhanced in macrophage-like RAW 264.7 cells exposed to nCB as compared to PEG-nCB.
source: In support of this, we found that the release of lactate dehydrogenase (LDH), an indicator of cytotoxicity, was enhanced in macrophage-like RAW 264.7 cells exposed to nCB as compared to PEG-nCB (Figure 4—figure supplement 2).
evidence: Supported by LDH assay data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2.

claim: Exposure to PEG-nCB resulted in attenuated recruitment of macrophages, neutrophils, and lymphocytes to the lung when compared with hydrophobic nCB.
source: Consistent with the failure to induce emphysema and cell death, exposure to PEG-nCB also resulted in attenuated recruitment of macrophages, neutrophils, and lymphocytes to the lung when compared with hydrophobic nCB (Figure 4D).
evidence: Supported by BAL fluid cell count data shown in Figure 4D.

claim: The reduction in inflammation in PEG-nCB-challenged mice was accompanied by reduced expression of Mmp9 and Mmp12 transcripts in BAL fluid cells as compared with nCB-challenged mice.
source: This reduction in inflammation was accompanied by reduced expression of Mmp9 and Mmp12 transcripts in BAL fluid cells as compared with nCB-challenged mice (Figure 4E,F).
evidence: Supported by qPCR data shown in Figure 4E,F.

claim: PEG-nCB-challenged mice showed reduced concentrations of pro-inflammatory cytokines and chemokines detected from freshly collected lung homogenates, including decreased IL-6 and IL-1β levels.
source: The markedly reduced inflammatory nature of PEG-nCB was further underscored by the reduced concentrations of pro-inflammatory cytokines and chemokines detected from freshly collected lung homogenates of PEG-nCB-challenged mice (Figure 4—figure supplement 3), including decreased IL-6 and IL-1β levels (Figure 4G,H).
evidence: Supported by ELISA and multiplex data shown in Figure 4G,H and Figure 4—figure supplement 3.

claim: PEG-nCB failed to induce lung Th17 cells when compared to nCB-exposed animals.
source: Critically, PEG-nCB failed to induce lung Th17 cells when compared to nCB-exposed animals (Figure 4I,J).
evidence: Supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 4I,J.

claim: The pro-inflammatory potential of nCB is intimately tied to its hydrophobic surface and ability to induce cytotoxicity of phagocytic cells.
source: Thus, the pro-inflammatory potential of nCB is intimately tied to its hydrophobic surface and ability to induce cytotoxicity of phagocytic cells.
evidence: Conclusion drawn from comparison of nCB and PEG-nCB effects.

claim: In response to nCB, but not PEG-nCB, reverse phase protein array (RPPA) identified the activation of several DNA damage (e.g., PARP, p-Chk2, p-ATM) and MAPK/Erk (p-ERK, p-MEK1/2)-response proteins.
source: In response to nCB, but not PEG-nCB, reverse phase protein array (RPPA) identified the activation of several DNA damage (e.g., PARP, p-Chk2, p-ATM) and MAPK/Erk (p-ERK, p-MEK1/2)-response proteins (Figure 5A and Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Supported by RPPA data shown in Figure 5A and Figure 5—figure supplement 1.

claim: nCB, but not PEG-nCB, induced DNA double strand breaks (DSB) as determined by phosphorylation of Histone 2AX (H2AX) on serine 129 (γH2AX).
source: Consistent with these data, we found that nCB, but not PEG-nCB, induced DNA double strand breaks (DSB) as determined by phosphorylation of Histone 2AX (H2AX) on serine 129 (γH2AX) (Figure 5B,C).
evidence: Supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 5B,C.

claim: The induction of DSB was inversely dependent on the size of nCB as progressively fewer DSB were observed with increasing nCB size.
source: Further, the induction of DSB was inversely dependent on the size of nCB as we observed progressively fewer DSB with increasing nCB size (Figure 5—figure supplement 2).
evidence: Supported by immunofluorescence data with different nCB sizes shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 2.

claim: Human monocyte-derived dendritic cells (MDDCs) treated with Nu7026, an inhibitor of the DNA-dependent protein kinase catalytic subunit, exhibited reduced IL-6 production in a dose-dependent manner in response to nCB but not LPS.
source: Human monocyte-derived dendritic cells (MDDCs) treated with Nu7026, an inhibitor of the DNA-dependent protein kinase catalytic subunit (Wilmore et al., 2004; Zhou et al., 2014), exhibited reduced IL-6 production in a dose-dependent manner in response to nCB but not LPS (Figure 5D).
evidence: Supported by ELISA data with inhibitor treatment shown in Figure 5D.

claim: In nCB-exposed RAW 264.7 cells, transfection of a specific siRNA against ataxia telangiectasia mutated (ATM) significantly reduced expression of IL-6 and TNFα.
source: Moreover, in nCB-exposed RAW 264.7 cells, transfection of a specific siRNA against ataxia telangiectasia mutated (ATM)—a serine–threonine kinase that coordinates repair of double-stranded DNA breaks (Guo et al., 2010)—significantly reduced expression of IL-6 and TNFα, two inflammatory cytokines that are induced through ATM (Figure 5—figure supplement 3).
evidence: Supported by qPCR data from siRNA knockdown experiments shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 3.

claim: ATM is a serine–threonine kinase that coordinates repair of double-stranded DNA breaks.
source: Moreover, in nCB-exposed RAW 264.7 cells, transfection of a specific siRNA against ataxia telangiectasia mutated (ATM)—a serine–threonine kinase that coordinates repair of double-stranded DNA breaks (Guo et al., 2010)—significantly reduced expression of IL-6 and TNFα, two inflammatory cytokines that are induced through ATM (Figure 5—figure supplement 3).
evidence: Supported by citation to published literature.

claim: IL-6 and TNFα are two inflammatory cytokines that are induced through ATM.
source: Moreover, in nCB-exposed RAW 264.7 cells, transfection of a specific siRNA against ataxia telangiectasia mutated (ATM)—a serine–threonine kinase that coordinates repair of double-stranded DNA breaks (Guo et al., 2010)—significantly reduced expression of IL-6 and TNFα, two inflammatory cytokines that are induced through ATM (Figure 5—figure supplement 3).
evidence: Inferred from siRNA knockdown experiments showing reduced cytokine expression.

claim: mDCs isolated from nCB-challenged mice promoted Th17 cell differentiation, which was significantly reduced in response to Nu7026 or Ku55933.
source: As expected, mDCs isolated from nCB-challenged mice promoted Th17 cell differentiation, which was significantly reduced in response to Nu7026 or Ku55933 (Figure 5E) while Th1 and Th2 cell differentiation remained unchanged (Figure 5—figure supplement 4).
evidence: Supported by ELISA data from co-culture experiments with inhibitors shown in Figure 5E.

claim: Nu7026 or Ku55933 treatment did not affect Th1 and Th2 cell differentiation in co-cultures with mDCs from nCB-challenged mice.
source: As expected, mDCs isolated from nCB-challenged mice promoted Th17 cell differentiation, which was significantly reduced in response to Nu7026 or Ku55933 (Figure 5E) while Th1 and Th2 cell differentiation remained unchanged (Figure 5—figure supplement 4).
evidence: Supported by ELISA data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 4.

claim: nCB-mediated DNA damage is required for the induction of pro-inflammatory cytokines in mDCs and Th17 cell differentiation.
source: Together, these findings suggest that nCB-mediated DNA damage is required for the induction of pro-inflammatory cytokines in mDCs and Th17 cell differentiation.
evidence: Conclusion drawn from inhibitor and siRNA experiments.

claim: nCB exposure in a dose- and time-dependent way increased phosphorylation of Erk.
source: Moreover, nCB exposure in a dose- and time-dependent way increased phosphorylation of Erk (Figure 5F), and similar inhibition of MEK1/2 with U0126, an inhibitor of MAP kinases (Newton et al., 2000), reduced IL-6 production in response to nCB exposure (Figure 5G).
evidence: Supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 5F.

claim: Inhibition of MEK1/2 with U0126 reduced IL-6 production in response to nCB exposure.
source: Moreover, nCB exposure in a dose- and time-dependent way increased phosphorylation of Erk (Figure 5F), and similar inhibition of MEK1/2 with U0126, an inhibitor of MAP kinases (Newton et al., 2000), reduced IL-6 production in response to nCB exposure (Figure 5G).
evidence: Supported by ELISA data with inhibitor treatment shown in Figure 5G.

claim: Hydrophobic nCB activates DNA damage responses and induces MAPK/Erk signaling coincident with the induction of Th17 responses.
source: Together, these findings indicate that hydrophobic nCB activates DNA damage responses and induces MAPK/Erk signaling coincident with the induction of Th17 responses.
evidence: Conclusion drawn from multiple signaling pathway experiments.

claim: The adaptor protein ASC (apoptosis-associated speck-like protein containing CARD) was shown to be required for inflammasome-dependent caspase-1–mediated conversion of pro-IL-1β to mature IL-1β.
source: The inflammasome detects danger signals released in response to cell injury and sterile inflammation and the adaptor protein ASC (apoptosis-associated speck-like protein containing CARD) was shown to be required for inflammasome-dependent caspase-1–mediated conversion of pro-IL-1β to mature IL-1β (Kono et al., 2012).
evidence: Supported by citation to published literature.

claim: In response to nCB exposure, lung CD11c+ mDCs increased IL-6 and IL-1β expression and RAW 264.7 cells released more LDH, consistent with the concept that nCB induces both sterile inflammation and necrotic cell death.
source: In response to nCB exposure, lung CD11c+ mDCs increased IL-6 and IL-1β expression and RAW 264.7 cells released more LDH, consistent with the concept that nCB induces both sterile inflammation and necrotic cell death.
evidence: Supported by cytokine and LDH data presented earlier.

claim: Pycard−/− mice showed attenuated emphysema when compared to WT mice treated identically with nCB.
source: When compared to WT mice treated identically, Pycard−/− mice showed attenuated emphysema (Figure 6A–C) and reduced macrophage, neutrophil, lymphocyte, and mDC infiltration into the lungs (Figure 6D,E).
evidence: Supported by histology, CT, and morphometry data shown in Figure 6A-C.

claim: Pycard−/− mice showed reduced macrophage, neutrophil, lymphocyte, and mDC infiltration into the lungs when compared to WT mice treated identically with nCB.
source: When compared to WT mice treated identically, Pycard−/− mice showed attenuated emphysema (Figure 6A–C) and reduced macrophage, neutrophil, lymphocyte, and mDC infiltration into the lungs (Figure 6D,E).
evidence: Supported by BAL fluid and flow cytometry data shown in Figure 6D,E.

claim: Lung mDCs of Pycard−/− mice produced less IL-6 and IL-1β and poorly activated splenic T cells to differentiate into Th17 cells when compared with WT mDC.
source: Consistently, lung mDCs of Pycard−/− mice produced less IL-6 and IL-1β and poorly activated splenic T cells to differentiate into Th17 cells when compared with WT mDC (Figure 6F–H).
evidence: Supported by ELISA data from cultured cells and co-culture experiments shown in Figure 6F-H.

claim: Freshly collected lung homogenates from Pycard−/− mice challenged with nCB showed reduced inflammatory chemokine production compared with WT mice.
source: Freshly collected lung homogenates from Pycard−/− mice challenged with nCB also showed reduced inflammatory chemokine production compared with WT mice (Figure 6—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Supported by multiplex assay data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1.

claim: The earliest immunological events induced by nCB include ASC activation and inflammasome assembly, which are in turn required for nCB-mediated Th17 responses and emphysema.
source: Thus, the earliest immunological events induced by nCB include ASC activation and inflammasome assembly, which are in turn required for nCB-mediated Th17 responses and emphysema.
evidence: Conclusion drawn from Pycard−/− mouse experiments.

claim: Evidence from experimental systems and human translational studies strongly support a role for chronic inflammation—and Th17 cells in particular—in the initiation and progression of emphysema in smokers.
source: Evidence from experimental systems and human translational studies strongly support a role for chronic inflammation—and Th17 cells in particular—in the initiation and progression of emphysema in smokers (Shan et al., 2012; Eppert et al., 2013; Kurimoto et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by citations to published literature.

claim: A characteristic feature of the anthracotic pigment of smokers' lungs is that such discoloration persists even long after smoking has ceased.
source: A characteristic feature of the anthracotic pigment of smokers' lungs is that such discoloration persists even long after smoking has ceased (Churg et al., 2005).
evidence: Supported by citation to published literature.

claim: This study is the first to clearly identify the anthracotic pigment as nCB and show that it accumulates specifically in human lung phagocytic cells.
source: Although several chemical identities have been proposed, our study is the first to clearly identify the anthracotic pigment as nCB and show that it accumulates specifically in human lung phagocytic cells.
evidence: Claim of novelty based on the study's findings.

claim: This study's functional studies are the first to show that nCB administered to the lungs in pathophysiologically relevant amounts can induce sterile inflammation and emphysema that is indistinguishable from disease induced by exposure to cigarette smoke in mice.
source: Our functional studies are also the first to show that nCB administered to the lungs in pathophysiologically relevant amounts can induce sterile inflammation and emphysema that is indistinguishable from disease induced by exposure to cigarette smoke in mice.
evidence: Claim of novelty based on the study's findings.

claim: nCB is likely the major component of smoke that causes long-term lung toxicity.
source: Thus, nCB is likely the major component of smoke that causes long-term lung toxicity.
evidence: Conclusion drawn from the study's findings.

claim: The findings have major implications regarding the safety of activities involving the chronic inhalation of smoke and the need to control the particulate composition of air.
source: Furthermore, our findings have major implications regarding the safety of activities involving the chronic inhalation of smoke and the need to control the particulate composition of air.
evidence: Implication drawn from the study's findings.

claim: Since nCB is used extensively in the rubber, plastics, and composites industries, the exposure levels should also be controlled in the workplace.
source: Since nCB is used extensively in the rubber, plastics, and composites industries, the exposure levels should also be controlled in the workplace.
evidence: Recommendation based on the study's findings and knowledge of industrial nCB use.

claim: Both chronic exposure to cigarette smoke and inhalation of nCB mediate similar inflammatory responses that are characterized by the activation of lung mDCs, differentiation and accumulation of Th17 cells, and lung parenchymal destruction (emphysema).
source: Both chronic exposure to cigarette smoke and inhalation of nCB mediate similar inflammatory responses that are characterized by the activation of lung mDCs, differentiation and accumulation of Th17 cells, and lung parenchymal destruction (emphysema) (Shan et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by comparison of smoke and nCB effects in the study and citation.

claim: The sterile inflammatory response to nCB is in part due to activation of the inflammasome pathway.
source: In part, this sterile inflammatory response to nCB is due to activation of the inflammasome pathway.
evidence: Supported by data from Pycard−/− mice.

claim: Inhaled nCB induces the production of IL-1β and IL-6, two pro-inflammatory cytokines that are required for mDC-mediated differentiation of Th17 cells and emphysema development.
source: Specifically, we found that inhaled nCB induces the production of IL-1β and IL-6, two pro-inflammatory cytokines that are required for mDC-mediated differentiation of Th17 cells and emphysema development.
evidence: Supported by cytokine measurements and functional studies in the manuscript.

claim: Inflammation persists and lung damage continues to accumulate even after smoking cessation due to the insoluble nature of nCB.
source: This inflammation persists and lung damage continues to accumulate even after smoking cessation due to the insoluble nature of nCB.
evidence: Inference based on nCB persistence data and long-term follow-up.

claim: Phagocytic lung cells that take up nCB most likely undergo cell death too rapidly for clearance mechanisms to operate efficiently.
source: Although readily taken up by phagocytic lung cells that could theoretically be expectorated or migrate out of the lungs via the lymphatics (Corry et al., 1984), these cells most likely undergo cell death too rapidly in response to nCB ingestion for any of these potential clearance mechanisms to operate efficiently.
evidence: Inference based on cytotoxicity data and persistence of nCB.

claim: nCB is released in the lung by the cells it kills, only to be taken up again and kill subsequent phagocytes, establishing an unending cycle of cell death.
source: The nCB is then released in the lung by the cells it kills, only to be taken up again and kill subsequent phagocytes. nCB thus establishes an unending cycle of cell death that, if sufficiently pronounced, will trigger activation of the inflammasome pathway in response to the release of danger-associated molecular patterns (DAMPs) from dying cells (Piccinini and Midwood, 2010).
evidence: Mechanistic model inferred from cytotoxicity and persistence data.

claim: nCB establishes an unending cycle of cell death that triggers activation of the inflammasome pathway in response to the release of danger-associated molecular patterns (DAMPs) from dying cells.
source: The nCB is then released in the lung by the cells it kills, only to be taken up again and kill subsequent phagocytes. nCB thus establishes an unending cycle of cell death that, if sufficiently pronounced, will trigger activation of the inflammasome pathway in response to the release of danger-associated molecular patterns (DAMPs) from dying cells (Piccinini and Midwood, 2010).
evidence: Mechanistic model combining data with citation about DAMPs.

claim: Immune responses both rapidly kill invading pathogens and solubilize antigenic and adjuvant-like pathogen-derived substances to facilitate their removal and thus terminate the potentially deleterious inflammation.
source: Immune responses both rapidly kill invading pathogens and solubilize antigenic and adjuvant-like pathogen-derived substances to facilitate their removal and thus terminate the potentially deleterious inflammation.
evidence: General immunological knowledge.

claim: Both fundamental immune functions of killing pathogens and solubilizing substances are thwarted in the context of nCB accumulation, leading to a perpetual cycle of lung inflammation and damage.
source: Both of these fundamental immune functions are thwarted in the context of nCB accumulation, leading to a perpetual cycle of lung inflammation and damage.
evidence: Inference based on the insoluble nature of nCB and persistence data.

claim: The findings raise concerns that other insoluble environmental nanoparticles may, if inhaled, accumulate in lung phagocytic cells and induce similar pathology.
source: Our findings, therefore, raise concerns that other insoluble environmental nanoparticles may, if inhaled, accumulate in lung phagocytic cells and induce similar pathology.
evidence: Speculation based on the study's findings.

claim: Inflammasome-activated IL-1β has been shown to play a major role in lung sterile inflammation induced by other nanoparticles associated with lung diseases.
source: In support of this, inflammasome-activated IL-1β has been shown to play a major role in lung sterile inflammation induced by other nanoparticles associated with lung diseases (Merget et al., 2002).
evidence: Supported by citation to published literature.

claim: ASC is required for the assembly of pro-caspase 1 in order to yield caspase 1 for the activation of pro-IL-1β to IL-1β.
source: ASC is required for the assembly of pro-caspase 1 in order to yield caspase 1 for the activation of pro-IL-1β to IL-1β (Franchi and Nunez, 2012).
evidence: Supported by citation to published literature.

claim: Inhaled nCB can activate the inflammasome pathway that results in production of mature IL-1β.
source: We show that inhaled nCB can activate the inflammasome pathway that results in production of mature IL-1β.
evidence: Supported by IL-1β measurements and Pycard−/− mouse data.

claim: Inflammasome sensors activated by nCB-damaged cells require ASC activation because lung mDCs isolated from Pycard−/− mice failed to increase IL-1β and showed attenuated Th17 responses.
source: In addition, inflammasome sensors activated by nCB-damaged cells require ASC activation because lung mDCs isolated from Pycard−/− mice failed to increase IL-1β and showed attenuated Th17 responses.
evidence: Supported by data from Pycard−/− mice.

claim: A critically important physical feature of nCB, accounting in large part for its pro-inflammatory potential, is its hydrophobic character.
source: A critically important physical feature of nCB, accounting in large part for its pro-inflammatory potential, is its hydrophobic character.
evidence: Conclusion drawn from comparison of nCB and PEG-nCB.

claim: Exposure to large quantities of hydrophobic nCB has been shown to induce cell injury, pyroptosis and generate reactive oxygen species (ROS) in cultured cells.
source: Exposure to large quantities of hydrophobic nCB has been shown to induce cell injury, pyroptosis and generate reactive oxygen species (ROS) in cultured cells (Reisetter et al., 2011).
evidence: Supported by citation to published literature.

claim: One particular characteristic of nCB that correlates with its toxicity is its large surface area; larger forms of elemental carbon have much less potential to induce cell injury.
source: One particular characteristic of nCB that correlates with its toxicity is its large surface area; larger forms of elemental carbon have much less potential to induce cell injury (Oberdörster et al., 2005) and, as we have shown here, damage DNA.
evidence: Supported by citation and data showing size-dependent DSB induction.

claim: A single burning cigarette can generate approximately 1012 particles that vary in size from 1 micron to a few nanometers in diameter.
source: A single burning cigarette can generate approximately 1012 particles that vary in size from 1 micron to a few nanometers in diameter (Sahu et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by citation to published literature.

claim: The deposition site of particulate matter in the lungs of smokers is governed largely by size, with larger particles depositing in the mouth and upper airway while smaller particles are deposited in progressively smaller and more distal airways.
source: The deposition site of particulate matter in the lungs of smokers is governed largely by size, with larger particles depositing in the mouth and upper airway while smaller particles are deposited in progressively smaller and more distal airways (Adam et al., 2006; Baker and Dixon, 2006).
evidence: Supported by citations to published literature.

claim: The nCB used in the study forms macro-aggregates in aqueous solution that fail to distribute evenly in the lung after intranasal challenge as does nCB delivered by smoke inhalation.
source: However, in aqueous solution, this material forms macro-aggregates that fail to distribute evenly in the lung after intranasal challenge as does nCB delivered by smoke inhalation.
evidence: Acknowledged limitation of the experimental approach.

claim: Although the study endeavored to deliver nCB to mice in amounts that matched actual burdens found in human lung, it is likely that the particle size and distribution of nCB acquired through smoke inhalation was not fully recapitulated.
source: Nonetheless, although we endeavored to deliver nCB to mice in amounts that matched actual burdens found in human lung, it is likely that we did not fully recapitulate the in vivo particle size and distribution of nCB acquired through smoke inhalation.
evidence: Acknowledged limitation of the experimental approach.

claim: Further studies are required to define how nCB size affects in vivo toxicity as defined in these studies.
source: Further studies are required to define how nCB size affects in vivo toxicity as defined in these studies.
evidence: Stated need for future research.

claim: Thermal and chemical analyses have shown that a combustion heat of 350–550°C yields black carbon (BC) that contains PAHs that are linked to inflammation.
source: Thermal and chemical analyses have shown that a combustion heat of 350–550°C yields black carbon (BC) that contains PAHs that are linked to inflammation (Bleck et al., 2006), but combustion at much higher temperatures (650–1100°C) produces PAH-free CB (Watson et al., 2005); we used this material heated to higher temperatures for intranasal administration in mice.
evidence: Supported by citations to published literature.

claim: Combustion at much higher temperatures (650–1100°C) produces PAH-free CB.
source: Thermal and chemical analyses have shown that a combustion heat of 350–550°C yields black carbon (BC) that contains PAHs that are linked to inflammation (Bleck et al., 2006), but combustion at much higher temperatures (650–1100°C) produces PAH-free CB (Watson et al., 2005); we used this material heated to higher temperatures for intranasal administration in mice.
evidence: Supported by citation to published literature.

claim: X-ray analysis of the melting of small metal particles has revealed the temperature distribution inside a burning cigarette as 850–920°C during active inhalation, decreasing to 700°C during the smoldering phase.
source: However, X-ray analysis of the melting of small metal particles has revealed the temperature distribution inside a burning cigarette as 850–920°C during active inhalation, decreasing to 700°C during the smoldering phase; this temperature regime is consistent with the creation of predominant CB during smoking (Baker, 1974).
evidence: Supported by citation to published literature.

claim: The temperature regime inside a burning cigarette is consistent with the creation of predominant CB during smoking.
source: However, X-ray analysis of the melting of small metal particles has revealed the temperature distribution inside a burning cigarette as 850–920°C during active inhalation, decreasing to 700°C during the smoldering phase; this temperature regime is consistent with the creation of predominant CB during smoking (Baker, 1974).
evidence: Inference based on temperature data and CB formation temperatures.

claim: As PAH-free CB recapitulates almost entirely the pathology induced by smoke exposure, sterile inflammation and pulmonary emphysema are primarily the result of CB accumulation in the lung and not that of BC or PAHs therein during smoking.
source: Moreover, as PAH-free CB recapitulates almost entirely the pathology induced by smoke exposure, we conclude that sterile inflammation and pulmonary emphysema are primarily the result of CB accumulation in the lung and not that of BC or PAHs therein during smoking.
evidence: Conclusion drawn from the study's findings using PAH-free nCB.

claim: Among signaling pathways that are important for APC activation and inflammation, phosphorylation of Erk was significantly upregulated in cells exposed to CB treatment in a dose- and time-dependent manner while phosphorylation of p38 or JNK were not changed.
source: Among signaling pathways that are important for APC activation and inflammation, we found that phosphorylation of Erk was significantly upregulated in cells exposed to CB treatment in a dose- and time-dependent manner while phosphorylation of p38 or JNK were not changed.
evidence: Supported by Western blot and RPPA data.

claim: The most notable, and unexpected, result of RPPA analysis was the upregulation of several DNA damage enzymes by nCB exposure.
source: The most notable, and unexpected, result of our RPPA analysis was the upregulation of several DNA damage enzymes by nCB exposure.
evidence: Observation from RPPA data.

claim: Nano-sized CB induces DSB in DNA as detected by the expression of γH2AX, an ATM-regulated pathway.
source: This led us to confirm that nano-sized CB induces DSB in DNA as detected by the expression of γH2AX, an ATM-regulated pathway.
evidence: Supported by immunofluorescence data.

claim: Larger forms of CB result in attenuation of DSB, indicating that the size of CB is an important factor in its genotoxicity.
source: We show that larger forms of CB result in attenuation of DSB, indicating that the size of CB is an important factor in its genotoxicity.
evidence: Supported by size-dependent DSB data.

claim: Activation of the DNA repair pathway is linked to the production of pro-inflammatory cytokines such as IL-6 and IL-1β that are required for Th17 differentiation.
source: Activation of this DNA repair pathway is in turn linked to the production of pro-inflammatory cytokines such as IL-6 and IL-1β that are required for Th17 differentiation.
evidence: Supported by inhibitor and siRNA experiments.

claim: MicroRNA-22 (miR-22) has been shown to be upregulated in lung APC of mice exposed to smoke or nCB and is critical in Th17 responses through activation of AP-1 complexes and histone deacetylase (HDAC) 4.
source: In addition, microRNA-22 (miR-22) has been shown to be upregulated in lung APC of mice exposed to smoke or nCB and is critical in Th17 responses through activation of AP-1 complexes and histone deacetylase (HDAC) 4 (Lu et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by citation to published literature.

claim: Together with DAMPs released by cells killed by nCB, nCB-induced DNA damage accounts for much of the inflammatory nature of nCB.
source: Thus, together with DAMPs released by cells killed by nCB, nCB-induced DNA damage accounts for much of the inflammatory nature of nCB.
evidence: Conclusion drawn from multiple experimental findings.

claim: The mechanism by which nCB cleaves DNA and the additional biological consequences of this adverse property remain active areas of investigation.
source: The mechanism by which nCB cleaves DNA and the additional biological consequences of this adverse property remain active areas of investigation in our laboratory.
evidence: Stated as ongoing research.

claim: Inhalation of cigarette smoke leads to the accumulation of nCB in airway APCs (macrophages and mDCs).
source: In summary, our findings show that inhalation of cigarette smoke leads to the accumulation of nCB in airway APCs (macrophages and mDCs).
evidence: Summary of the study's findings.

claim: Insoluble nCB promotes perpetual Th17 cell-mediated lung inflammation in part through the double-stranded cleavage of nuclear DNA.
source: This insoluble material promotes perpetual Th17 cell-mediated lung inflammation in part through the double-stranded cleavage of nuclear DNA.
evidence: Summary of the study's findings.

claim: These findings largely explain the persistent and incurable nature of smoking-related lung disease.
source: These findings largely explain the persistent and incurable nature of smoking-related lung disease.
evidence: Conclusion drawn from the study's findings.

claim: No medical means of removing accumulated lung nCB exists.
source: Because no medical means of removing accumulated lung nCB exists, our findings underscore the need for all individuals and societies to minimize the production of and exposure to smoke-related particulate air pollution and industrial nCB.
evidence: Stated as current medical limitation.

claim: The findings underscore the need for all individuals and societies to minimize the production of and exposure to smoke-related particulate air pollution and industrial nCB.
source: Because no medical means of removing accumulated lung nCB exists, our findings underscore the need for all individuals and societies to minimize the production of and exposure to smoke-related particulate air pollution and industrial nCB.
evidence: Recommendation based on the study's findings.
